Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: Epidemiology & Risk Factors in Head & Neck Cancer
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is not one disease. It is a family of cancers that start in the lining of the mouth, throat, and voice box, and each subsite has its own biology. Start with the subsite, because the subsite predicts the cause, the pattern of spread, the staging system, and the treatment.

Start With the Subsite

SubsiteMain driversThink first aboutWhy it matters
Oral cavityTobacco, alcohol, smokeless tobacco, betel nut; sun for the lipDepth of invasion and the mandibleSurgery usually comes first; radiation is mostly adjuvant
OropharynxHPV, or tobacco and alcoholp16 statusp16 decides the staging system, and the site is often treated with definitive RT or transoral surgery
NasopharynxEBV, salt-preserved fish, genetics and geographyThe skull base and cranial nervesTreatment is radiation-centered; surgery is for salvage
Larynx / hypopharynxTobacco and alcoholGlottic vs supraglottic, and cord mobilityLymphatic drainage differs by compartment, and the goal is a functional larynx

Less common contributors for any subsite: immunosuppression (HIV, organ transplant) and inherited syndromes such as Fanconi anemia.

Leukoplakia (a white patch) and erythroplakia (a red patch) are premalignant. Any nonhealing white or red oral lesion gets a biopsy, not reassurance.

Oropharynx: Two Diseases, One Name

Oropharynx cancer used to look just like oral cavity cancer: an older heavy smoker and drinker. Over the past few decades, HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer has become the dominant form, and the two look almost like mirror images.

HPV-positiveHPV-negative
AgeYoungerOlder
Smoking/alcoholNon- or light smokerHeavy smoker and drinker
Other risk factorSexual exposure (number of oral sex partners)Not linked to sexual behavior
Favored subsiteTonsil / base of tongueNo particular preference
Typical presentationSmall primary, cystic level II nodeLarger primary, symptoms from the primary
Molecular driverp16 overexpressedp53 mutation
PrognosisBetter, stage for stageWorse

Why p16 Is the Test for HPV

  • High-risk HPV makes the E7 oncoprotein, which inactivates pRb. pRb normally keeps p16 turned down, so p16 becomes overexpressed.
  • p16 is a simple immunohistochemistry stain, so p16 positivity is the clinical surrogate for HPV in the oropharynx.
  • That surrogate is what puts a patient into the HPV-associated oropharynx staging system in AJCC 8th edition.
Why it matters for staging
Two staging systems

AJCC 8th edition stages p16-positive and p16-negative oropharynx cancer separately, with more favorable stage groups for p16-positive disease.

Why it matters for treatment
Better prognosis, same treatment

The better prognosis is why trials ask whether these patients can get less intense treatment. Off trial, they still get standard treatment (see Treatment Paradigms).

Why the Risk Factor Changes What You Ask

The history points you toward a biology before the biopsy comes back, and that tells you what to look for next.

Patient 1
Older heavy smoker, oral tongue ulcer
  • Think conventional (HPV-negative) HNSCC.
  • Inspect and palpate the whole oral cavity; field cancerization means second lesions happen.
  • Ask about depth of invasion and mandible involvement.
  • Expect surgery to be central, with radiation decided by the pathology.
Patient 2
Younger light smoker, cystic level II node
  • Think HPV-associated oropharynx cancer.
  • Send p16 on the node or primary.
  • Search carefully for a small tonsil or base of tongue primary.
  • Stage with the p16-positive oropharynx system.

Nasopharynx: Why It Behaves Differently

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is driven by EBV, salt-preserved fish, and genetics, and it is endemic in southern China, Southeast Asia, and North Africa. Endemic disease is nearly always the nonkeratinizing, undifferentiated type (WHO type III). What matters more on a Rad Onc rotation is why it behaves differently from other H&N cancers:

Skull base location

It sits right under the skull base, so it reaches bone and cranial nerves early.

Rich lymphatics

Spreads early to the retropharyngeal nodes and to levels II and V, often on both sides.

EBV biology

Plasma EBV DNA works as a tumor marker for staging and response.

Radiosensitive

It responds well to radiation and chemotherapy, while surgery is hard to do well here.

Put together, that is why NPC is treated with radiation-based therapy, and surgery is mostly for salvage (see Treatment Paradigms).

Clinical Pearl

Always know a patient's p16/HPV status before talking about prognosis in oropharynx cancer. Different patient, different biology, different staging system.

High-Yield Summary
  • Start with the subsite, because it predicts the cause, the pattern of spread, the staging system, and the treatment.
  • Oral cavity, larynx, and hypopharynx cancers are driven by tobacco and alcohol, and resectable oral cavity cancer usually goes to surgery first.
  • Oropharyngeal cancer is now two diseases: HPV-positive (younger, lighter smokers, better prognosis) and HPV-negative (older, heavy smokers and drinkers).
  • p16 staining is the clinical surrogate for HPV, and it decides which staging system an oropharynx cancer uses.
  • Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is driven by EBV, sits under the skull base, spreads to nodes on both sides early, and is treated mainly with radiation.

Anatomy.title: Head & Neck Anatomy
Anatomy.html:
Head and neck radiation oncology is basically geography. Which structures a tumor can reach decides the stage, the surgery, and the shape of the radiation field. This page goes site by site: oral cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx, then larynx. For every structure, ask one question: if the tumor reaches this, what happens to the patient or to the stage? Lymph node drainage has its own section next.

How to use this page
Explore, then quiz

Each site has an interactive plate. Click through it in Explore mode, then switch to Quiz mode. The Patterns of Local Spread table then ties each site to its symptoms and stage.

Why it matters
Symptoms stage the tumor

A fixed vocal cord makes a larynx cancer T3. A cranial nerve palsy makes a nasopharynx cancer T4. The neuro exam is part of staging.

Oral Cavity

The oral cavity runs from the lips back to the circumvallate papillae (on the tongue) and the junction of the hard and soft palate (on the roof). It has seven subsites:

SubsiteWhat to know
LipLinked to sun exposure. Lower lip drains to level I.
Oral tongue (anterior 2/3)The most common oral cavity site, usually the lateral tongue.
Floor of mouthSits on the mylohyoid; close to the mandible and the lingual nerve.
Buccal mucosaInner cheek. Linked to betel nut chewing.
Gingiva / alveolar ridgeSits right on bone, so mandible invasion happens early.
Retromolar trigoneBehind the last lower molar. Reaches the pterygoids early (trismus).
Hard palateBony roof. Drains to II-IV, not level I.
The circumvallate papillae split the tongue: in front is oral tongue (oral cavity), behind is base of tongue (oropharynx).

That line matters because the two sides are different diseases. Oral tongue cancer is treated with surgery first. Base of tongue cancer is often HPV-driven and is frequently treated with radiation.

Nerves & Presentations: Oral Cavity

If the tumor reaches...The patient noticesWhy a Rad Onc cares
Lingual nerve (CN V3)Numb anterior tongueA common route for perineural invasion (PNI). Get an MRI for perineural spread; PNI on pathology is an indication for adjuvant RT, and the field may follow the nerve.
Inferior alveolar / mental nerve (CN V3)Numb chin or lower lipThink mandible invasion or PNI. Through cortical bone is T4a.
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)Tongue deviates toward the lesionSignals deep or posterior spread; check depth of invasion and base of tongue extension on MRI.
  • PNI tracks backward along CN V3 toward the foramen ovale and skull base. It can carry tumor beyond what is visible, which is why the radiation field may extend along the nerve path.
  • Taste rides with the lingual nerve (chorda tympani), which is one reason taste changes are almost universal during H&N RT.

Oropharynx

The oropharynx sits directly behind the oral cavity, between the soft palate above and the vallecula below. It has four subsites:

1
Palatine Tonsil

The most common site of HPV-positive cancer.

2
Base of Tongue

Posterior 1/3 of the tongue. Tumors can be small and hidden and still present with a big neck node.

3
Soft Palate

The roof. Midline, so both sides of the neck are at risk.

4
Posterior Pharyngeal Wall

Midline too. Drains to the retropharyngeal nodes.

Anterior
Circumvallate papillae and anterior tonsillar pillars
Superior
Soft palate (above it is the nasopharynx)
Inferior
Vallecula and tip of the epiglottis (below it are the larynx and hypopharynx)
Lateral
Tonsillar fossae and pillars; beyond them the parapharyngeal space and pterygoid muscles
Posterior
Posterior pharyngeal wall and prevertebral muscles

Nerves & Presentations: Oropharynx

  • Painless neck mass. The most common presentation of HPV-positive cancer, often a cystic level II node with a small primary.
  • Referred otalgia via CN IX. The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the tonsil and base of tongue and also the middle ear. Ear pain with a normal ear exam means look at the tonsil and base of tongue.
  • Trismus. Means lateral spread into the pterygoid muscles, which is advanced (T4) disease.

Nasopharynx

The nasopharynx is the top of the pharynx, directly under the skull base and behind the nasal cavity. Its location explains why it presents late, reaches cranial nerves early, and is not treated with surgery.

Anterior
Posterior choanae / back of the nasal septum
Posterior
C1-C2 and the prevertebral muscles
Superior
Skull base (sphenoid and clivus)
Inferior
Soft palate
Lateral
Eustachian tube opening, torus tubarius, and the fossa of Rosenmüller
Most nasopharyngeal carcinomas start in the fossa of Rosenmüller, the recess just behind the torus tubarius.

Nerves & Presentations: Nasopharynx

Think of NPC presentations in four groups:

1
Neck Mass

The most common presentation. Often bilateral, often level II and V, with retropharyngeal nodes first.

2
Ear

Unilateral serous otitis media in an adult from eustachian tube blockage. Scope the nasopharynx.

3
Nose

Nasal obstruction, bloody discharge, or epistaxis from tumor growing forward.

4
Cranial Nerves

Skull base spread. Any cranial nerve involvement is T4.

Route of spreadNerves at riskSymptom
Up through the skull base into the cavernous sinusCN III, IV, V1, V2, VIDiplopia (CN VI is the most commonly affected nerve), facial numbness
Along V3 through the foramen ovaleCN V3Numb jaw/cheek, jaw weakness
Back and lateral into the parapharyngeal / retrostyloid spaceCN IX, X, XI, XII and the sympathetic chainHoarseness, dysphagia, shoulder weakness, tongue deviation, Horner syndrome
Self-check: a 50-year-old with double vision, a one-sided ear effusion, and a level V node. Where is the primary?▾

Nasopharynx. The ear effusion is eustachian tube blockage, the double vision is CN VI from cavernous sinus spread (making it T4), and level V is a classic NPC nodal station. Next: nasopharyngoscopy with biopsy, MRI of the skull base, and plasma EBV DNA.

Larynx

The larynx is three compartments stacked on top of each other, and each one behaves like a different disease. Use the Coronal View above to see them top to bottom.

CompartmentExtentLymphaticsPresents with
SupraglottisTip of epiglottis to the ventricle (epiglottis, false cords, arytenoids, AE folds)Rich, both sides of the neckDysphagia, sore throat, neck mass (found late)
GlottisTrue vocal cords + anterior/posterior commissuresAlmost noneEarly hoarseness (found early)
SubglottisUnder the true cords to the bottom of the cricoidRich, includes level VIStridor, airway symptoms
The glottis has almost no lymphatics. That is why early glottic cancer is treated without the neck, and supraglottic cancer is not.
Space 1
Pre-epiglottic space

Fat in front of the epiglottis. A route for supraglottic cancer to spread deep.

Space 2
Paraglottic space

Fat and muscle lateral to the cords, inside the thyroid cartilage. Tumor here can fix the cord and reach the cartilage.

CartilageWhy it matters
ThyroidThe shield around the larynx. Tumor that breaks through it has left the larynx.
CricoidThe only complete ring; the bottom of the larynx. Its lower edge is also a staging landmark for nasopharynx nodes.
ArytenoidsAnchor the back of the cords. Invasion here can fix the cord.

Nerves & Presentations: Larynx

  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve (CN X). Supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except the cricothyroid. It runs in the tracheoesophageal groove, so thyroid disease, subglottic tumor, and level VI nodes can injure it. Result: hoarseness and a paralyzed cord.
  • Referred otalgia via CN X. The auricular branch of the vagus supplies the ear canal. Ear pain in a supraglottic or hypopharyngeal cancer suggests deep invasion.

Patterns of Local Spread

This is where anatomy turns into staging. Read each row left to right: where the tumor starts, what it grows into, what the patient notices, and what that does to the stage.

PrimaryGrows intoClinical findingStaging consequence
Oral tongueDeep into tongue musclePain, reduced tongue movementGreater depth of invasion raises T (T2-T3)
Gingiva / floor of mouthMandibleLoose teeth, numb chinThrough cortical bone = T4a
Retromolar trigoneMasticator space / pterygoidsTrismusT4b (generally unresectable)
TonsilMedial pterygoid, then lateral pterygoid and skull baseTrismusMedial pterygoid = T4 (T4a if p16-negative); lateral pterygoid or skull base = T4b if p16-negative
Base of tongueVallecula and epiglottis, then the larynxDysphagia, muffled voiceLingual epiglottis = T3; larynx = T4 (T4a if p16-negative)
NasopharynxParapharyngeal space, then skull base, then cavernous sinusEar effusion, then headache, then diplopiaParapharyngeal = T2; bone = T3; intracranial or cranial nerve = T4
Glottis / supraglottisParaglottic or pre-epiglottic spaceHoarseness, fixed cordT3
LarynxThrough the outer thyroid cartilage into strap muscles or thyroidNeck mass over the larynx, airway symptomsT4a; prevertebral space or carotid encasement = T4b
T4a usually means resectable but locally advanced. T4b usually means a structure surgeons can't safely take: the masticator space, skull base, prevertebral space, or the carotid.

Anatomy You Need to Recognize on a CT Simulation Scan

You will not be contouring alone, but you should be able to scroll through a planning CT and know roughly what you're looking at. These are the structures that come up when the team talks about targets and organs at risk.

StructureHow to find it on axial CTWhy it comes up
MandibleBright U-shaped bone around the tongue; the ramus runs up toward the earOsteoradionecrosis risk; invasion changes surgery
Oral cavityTongue and floor of mouth inside the mandible archMucositis and taste
Parotid glandsJust behind and lateral to the mandibular ramus, in front of the ear; darker (fattier) than muscleThe main gland to spare for dry mouth
Submandibular glandsUnder the body of the mandible, in level IbSaliva at rest; often near the nodal targets
Pharyngeal constrictorsThin muscle band wrapping the back of the throat, in front of the spineSwallowing
LarynxAir column inside the thyroid cartilage, below the hyoidVoice, swallowing, edema
Spinal cordInside the vertebral canalA hard limit in every plan
BrainstemAbove the foramen magnum, in front of the cerebellum, on the top slicesA hard limit, especially for nasopharynx
Carotid arteriesBright round vessels (with contrast) beside the jugular veins, next to levels II-IVEncasement can make a tumor unresectable
Thyroid glandBright gland wrapped around the trachea below the cricoidHypothyroidism after neck RT
Brachial plexusBetween the anterior and middle scalene muscles, lower neck down to the clavicleNear low-neck nodal targets

Nerves at Risk in the Neck

These nerves come up with neck dissections, bulky nodes, and radiation toxicity. Know where each one runs and what happens when it is injured.

NerveWhere it runsInjury looks like
Spinal accessory (CN XI)Crosses level IIb and VShoulder drop, weak abduction, winged scapula
Marginal mandibular (CN VII)Under the mandible, near level IbAsymmetric lower lip when smiling
Hypoglossal (CN XII)Crosses level II just above the carotid bifurcationTongue deviates toward the injured side
Vagus (CN X)Inside the carotid sheathHoarseness, aspiration
PhrenicOn the anterior scalene, deep to level IV / VbElevated hemidiaphragm
Sympathetic chainBehind the carotid sheath, near the retropharyngeal nodesHorner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis)
High-Yield Summary
  • The circumvallate papillae divide the oral tongue (oral cavity, surgery first) from the base of tongue (oropharynx, often HPV-driven).
  • The nasopharynx sits under the skull base and most cancers start in the fossa of Rosenmüller, so a one-sided ear effusion or a cranial nerve palsy is a red flag.
  • The glottis has almost no lymphatics, so early glottic cancer is treated without the neck, while supraglottic cancer is not.
  • Local spread maps to stage: a fixed cord or paraglottic invasion is T3 in the larynx, trismus from the masticator space is T4b in the oral cavity, and a cranial nerve palsy is T4 in the nasopharynx.
  • On a planning CT, you should be able to find the mandible, parotids, submandibular glands, constrictors, larynx, spinal cord, brainstem, carotids, thyroid, and brachial plexus.

Lymph Nodes.title: The Cervical Lymph Node Level System
Lymph Nodes.html:
Nearly every head and neck cancer drains into a predictable set of neck lymph nodes, and surgeons, radiologists, and radiation oncologists all describe them with the same level system (I through VII). That shared language lets you:

  • Read a radiology report and know exactly which nodes are enlarged.
  • Read an op note and know which nodes were removed in a neck dissection.
  • Draw an elective nodal volume that covers the nodes at risk without treating the whole neck.

This section moves from where the lymph nodes are to why we treat the ones we treat.

The Cervical Lymph Node Levels

LevelNameBoundariesClassic primaries
IaSubmentalBetween the anterior bellies of the digastrics; mandible to hyoidLower lip, anterior tongue, anterior floor of mouth
IbSubmandibularUnder the body of the mandible; contains the submandibular glandMost oral cavity sites
IIUpper jugularSkull base to the bottom of the hyoid; IIa in front of the IJV, IIb behind itAlmost every site; the most commonly involved level
IIIMid jugularHyoid to the bottom of the cricoidOropharynx, larynx, hypopharynx
IVLower jugularCricoid to the clavicleLarynx, hypopharynx, subglottis
VPosterior triangleBehind the SCM, skull base to clavicle; Va upper, Vb lowerNasopharynx
VICentral compartmentHyoid to sternal notch, between the carotids; includes the Delphian nodeSubglottis, thyroid
VIIRetropharyngeal (Rouvière)Behind the pharyngeal wall, in front of the prevertebral fasciaAny pharynx (naso-, oro-, hypo-)
Two bones and one cartilage divide the jugular chain: the hyoid (II above, III below), the cricoid (III above, IV below), and the clavicle (bottom of IV).

How the Primary Site Predicts Nodal Risk

Lymph spreads in a predictable order, usually from the top of the neck down, one level at a time. Learn the pattern for each site rather than a fixed list. Click between subsites below to see how the levels at risk change.

Oral Cavity

Think I → II → III. Anterior sites (lower lip, anterior tongue, anterior floor of mouth) add level Ia. Tumors near the midline can drain to both sides.

Oropharynx

Think II → III → IV, plus the retropharyngeal nodes. Then ask: tonsil or base of tongue? Lateralized or near midline?

Nasopharynx

Think retropharyngeal + II + V, on both sides. The one site where level V is routinely part of the picture.

Larynx

Glottis is not supraglottis. Early glottic cancer has almost no nodal risk; supraglottic cancer drains to II-IV on both sides. Subglottic spread brings in level VI.

Levels II-IV are common components of elective neck treatment, but the exact nodal volume and laterality depend on the primary site, its extent, and the risk of occult nodal disease. The factors that move the volume up or down:

FactorHow it changes the nodal volume
Primary subsiteSets the basic drainage pattern (above)
Laterality and midline involvementDecides one side or both (below)
Primary extentSpread into a new subsite brings in that subsite's drainage (e.g., subglottic extension adds level VI)
Involved nodesA positive node raises the risk in the levels next to it, so those levels are more likely to be included
Prior surgeryAfter a neck dissection, the pathology (number of nodes, ENE) guides what still needs treatment
Definitive vs postoperativeDefinitive RT treats the gross nodes plus the at-risk levels; postoperative RT treats the operative bed and the at-risk levels

One Side or Both?

Usually both sides
Bilateral neck

Midline or near-midline primaries: base of tongue, soft palate, posterior pharyngeal wall, supraglottis, nasopharynx. Also any patient with nodes on both sides.

Often one side
Ipsilateral neck

A well-lateralized tonsil cancer without base of tongue or soft palate involvement, and some well-lateralized oral cavity cancers.

Self-check: why can early glottic cancer skip the neck, but early supraglottic cancer can't?▾

The glottis has almost no lymphatics, while the supraglottis drains richly to both sides of the neck. Early glottic cancer is treated to the larynx alone; supraglottic cancer gets elective treatment of both sides of the neck.

Involved vs Elective Nodes

This is the bridge from anatomy to a radiation plan. The team separates nodes that definitely have cancer from nodes that might, and treats them differently.

1
GTVn

Gross tumor volume, nodal. A node you can see or feel: enlarged, necrotic, or PET-avid. Gets the full (definitive) dose.

2
CTV

Clinical target volume. Regions at risk for microscopic disease: a margin around the involved node (higher risk) and the elective levels (lower risk, lower dose).

3
PTV

Planning target volume. The CTV plus a small margin for daily setup variation.

Gross nodes get the full dose because we know cancer is there. Elective levels get a lower dose because microscopic disease takes less dose to control.
Clinical Pearl

Retropharyngeal (level VII) nodes are deep and can't be felt on exam, which makes them easy to forget. They are part of the at-risk volume for pharyngeal primaries, especially the nasopharynx.

High-Yield Summary
  • The hyoid separates level II from III, the cricoid separates III from IV, and the clavicle is the bottom of IV.
  • Lymph spreads in a predictable order by site: oral cavity to I, II, and III; oropharynx to II, III, IV, and the retropharyngeal nodes; nasopharynx to the retropharyngeal nodes, II, and V on both sides.
  • Levels II to IV are common parts of elective neck treatment, but the exact volume depends on the site, its extent, the involved nodes, and the risk of occult disease.
  • Midline primaries and bilateral nodes get both sides of the neck treated, while a well-lateralized tonsil cancer can often be treated on one side.
  • Gross nodes (GTVn) get the full dose, elective levels at risk for microscopic disease get a lower dose, and the PTV adds a margin for setup.

Imaging.title: Imaging in Head & Neck Cancer
Imaging.html:
Head and neck cancer relies on three imaging tools: CT, MRI, and PET/CT. Don't memorize them as a list of facts. Start with the question you need answered, then pick the study that answers it. The answers become the stage and the radiation plan.

Choose Imaging Based on the Question

The questionBest toolWhy
1. Where is the primary, and how far does it extend?Contrast CT or MRI, depending on siteMRI shows soft tissue best (oral cavity depth, nasopharynx, oropharynx); CT is fast and good for most neck staging
2. Is there bone or cartilage invasion?CT especially, with MRI as a complementCT shows cortical erosion of the mandible and laryngeal cartilage well; MRI can show marrow and soft-tissue changes
3. Is there skull-base or perineural spread?MRIShows nerves, foramina, and marrow at the skull base
4. Are there occult nodal or distant metastases?PET/CT when indicated (usually locally advanced disease)Whole-body survey; CT or MRI is still needed for local anatomy and planning
5. Is there residual disease after treatment?PET/CT about 12 weeks after chemoradiationActive tumor is FDG-avid, while scar usually is not; a negative scan can spare a neck dissection
SiteUsual study for the primaryWhy
Oral cavityMRI, with CT for the mandibleDepth of invasion is a soft-tissue measurement
OropharynxCT or MRISoft-tissue extent; look for loss of fat planes
NasopharynxMRISkull base and perineural spread
LarynxCTCartilage invasion helps define T-stage

How a Rad Onc Reads the Imaging

Go through every scan in the same order. By the end you should be able to say what the tumor touches, which nodes are involved, and what that means for treatment.

1
Primary

Where exactly? How big? How far along the mucosa, and how deep?

2
Adjacent structures

Bone? Cartilage? Muscle? Skull base? Any sign of perineural spread?

3
Nodes

Which levels? One side or both? Size, necrosis, signs of ENE?

4
Distant disease

Was a PET/CT done? Look at the lungs, liver, and bone.

5
Treatment implications

Resectable? Definitive RT? One side of the neck or both? Which critical structures sit next to the target?

Oral Cavity Imaging

  • MRI is preferred for the primary because depth of invasion (DOI), the biggest driver of oral cavity T-stage, is a soft-tissue measurement.
  • CT is particularly useful for mandible cortex erosion, which makes the tumor T4a.
  • Check whether the tumor crosses the oral tongue / base of tongue line or the midline, since both change the surgery and the neck coverage.

Nasopharynx Imaging

  • The earliest sign is often subtle: effacement of the fossa of Rosenmüller.
  • MRI is the study of choice for the primary and for skull-base, cavernous sinus, or perineural extension, which decide T3 vs T4.
  • Look for retropharyngeal nodes, which can't be felt on exam.

Larynx Imaging

CT is the workhorse for the larynx because it shows the cartilage and the paraglottic and pre-epiglottic fat well, and those findings help define T-stage. MRI can add information when cartilage invasion is uncertain. Oropharyngeal tumors, by comparison, show up on CT as an asymmetric enhancing mass, and advanced disease shows loss of the normal fat planes around it.

Cartilage Invasion and the Laryngeal T-Stage Ladder

StageImaging correlate
T3Cord fixation, paraglottic or pre-epiglottic space invasion, or inner cortex of the thyroid cartilage
T4aThrough the outer cortex of the thyroid cartilage, cricoid invasion, or spread outside the larynx (trachea, strap muscles, thyroid)
T4bPrevertebral space, mediastinum, or carotid encasement

Reading Lymph Nodes on Imaging

Suspicious node
Any of these
  • Short axis >10 mm
  • Loss of the fatty hilum
  • Cystic or necrotic change
Extranodal extension (ENE)
Tumor through the capsule
  • Loss of the fat plane around the node
  • Irregular capsular enhancement
  • Ill-defined margins

Imaging can only suggest ENE; pathology confirms it. It matters because ENE on pathology after surgery is one of the two indications for postoperative chemoradiation.

1
HPV+ Oropharynx

Early spread to level II, often cystic. A cystic level II node can be the first finding even when the primary is tiny or hidden.

2
Nasopharynx

First echelon is retropharyngeal, but it can skip straight to level II. Levels II and V are the most common neck levels.

Perineural Spread

Perineural spread is macroscopic and visible on imaging, unlike microscopic perineural invasion (PNI) seen only on pathology. It most often follows the trigeminal (V) and facial (VII) nerves, and when it's present the radiation field follows the nerve back toward the skull base.

MRI signWhat you see
Nerve thickeningThe nerve is bigger than the other side
Foraminal wideningThe skull base foramen it passes through is enlarged
Loss of perineural fatThe normal fat around the nerve is gone
Abnormal enhancementThe nerve enhances after contrast
Clinical Pearl

A small or hidden oropharyngeal primary with a cystic level II node is a classic HPV-positive presentation. Don't call a cystic neck node in an adult benign until this is ruled out.

High-Yield Summary
  • Pick the scan by the question: CT or MRI for the primary, CT especially for bone and cartilage, MRI for skull base and perineural spread, and PET/CT for occult nodes, distant disease, and response after treatment.
  • Read every scan in the same order: the primary, the structures next to it, the nodes, distant disease, and what it all means for treatment.
  • A suspicious node is larger than 10 mm in short axis, has lost its fatty hilum, or is cystic or necrotic.
  • A cystic level II node with a small or hidden primary is a classic HPV-positive oropharynx presentation.
  • In the larynx, inner thyroid cartilage invasion is T3 and outer cortex breakthrough or cricoid invasion is T4a.

Workup & Staging.title: Head & Neck Cancer: Workup & Staging
Workup & Staging.html:
This page answers one question: here's a new head and neck patient; what do I need to know before I can recommend treatment? The first four sections gave you the biology, the anatomy, the nodes, and the imaging. Workup is where they come together into a complete oncologic diagnosis. You don't need the whole AJCC manual memorized; the full site-by-site tables are at the bottom of the page.

StepWhat you doWhat you're looking for
1. Clinical examLook at and palpate the oral cavity and oropharynx; flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy in clinic; full cranial nerve exam; examine every neck levelSize and extent of the primary, vocal cord movement, cranial nerve deficits, trismus, palpable nodes
2. Tissue diagnosisBiopsy of the primary or FNA of a neck nodeConfirms squamous cell carcinoma (or another histology); p16 for any oropharynx primary or node of unknown primary
3. ImagingCT neck with contrast and/or MRI by site; PET/CT when indicated (usually locally advanced disease)Primary extent, bone or cartilage, skull base, nodes, distant disease (see Imaging)
4. PathologyFrom the biopsy, and in full from the surgical specimen if the patient has surgeryMargins, DOI, PNI, LVSI, ENE, and the number of positive nodes. These decide adjuvant treatment
5. Functional assessmentDental evaluation, nutrition, speech and swallow, performance status and comorbidities, smokingExtract bad teeth before RT; baseline swallowing and weight; whether the patient can tolerate surgery or cisplatin
6. StageAssign T, N, and M using the right site-specific AJCC systemWhich system applies (p16? nasopharynx?), and the features that push the stage up
7. Multidisciplinary decisionTumor board with surgery, radiation oncology, medical oncology, radiology, pathology, and supportive servicesSurgery? Definitive RT? Chemoradiation? Systemic therapy? A clinical trial?
SiteAdd this to the workup
Oral cavityMRI (or CT) to estimate depth of invasion; look for mandible invasion
Oropharynxp16 IHC (HPV surrogate) on the primary or node; smoking pack-years
NasopharynxPlasma EBV DNA, MRI of the skull base, EBV (EBER) testing on the biopsy
Larynx / hypopharynxDirect laryngoscopy under anesthesia; assess cord mobility and airway

What Changes the Stage, Site by Site

Every site uses T, N, and M, but each one has a feature you must know because it changes the stage. Learn this table first, then the details below.

SiteStaging feature you must know
Oral cavityDepth of invasion is built into T
Oropharynxp16 status decides which staging system to use
NasopharynxIts own T and N rules: T by where it spread, N by side and height
LarynxCord mobility and spread into spaces and cartilage
Non-HPV H&N (oral cavity, larynx, hypopharynx, p16-negative oropharynx)Conventional T and N, with ENE built into N

T-Stage: Size, Then Invasion

TGeneral rule
T1About ≤2 cm
T2About >2 to 4 cm
T3>4 cm, or a site-specific deep feature (DOI in the oral cavity, cord fixation in the larynx)
T4aInvades nearby structures but still resectable (bone, cartilage, skin)
T4bVery advanced, generally unresectable (carotid encasement, prevertebral space, skull base, masticator space, mediastinum)

N-Stage: Number, Side, Size, and ENE

Clinical N for the oral cavity, larynx, hypopharynx, and p16-negative oropharynx:

NNodes (all ENE-negative unless noted)
N0None
N1Single ipsilateral, ≤3 cm
N2aSingle ipsilateral, >3 to 6 cm
N2bMultiple ipsilateral, none >6 cm
N2cBilateral or contralateral, none >6 cm
N3aAny node >6 cm
N3bClinically obvious ENE (skin involvement, fixed to muscle or nerve)
Pathologic N after a neck dissection: what's different?▾

After surgery the pathologist can see microscopic ENE, so pathologic N shifts up. A single ipsilateral node ≤3 cm with ENE becomes pN2a. A node >3 cm with ENE, or multiple or contralateral nodes with any ENE, becomes pN3b. Whatever the stage, ENE on pathology means adding chemo to postoperative radiation.

M is simply M0 or M1. The lungs are the most common distant site, which is why the chest is always imaged. Stage groups for each site are in the tables at the bottom.

Oral Cavity: Depth of Invasion

  • The only H&N site where depth of invasion (DOI) is built into the T-stage. A small but deep tumor can outstage a large, superficial one.
  • The DOI cutoffs to remember are 5 mm and 10 mm.
  • Bone invasion counts as T4a only if it goes through cortical bone. Superficial erosion of a tooth socket is not enough.

Oropharynx: p16 First

Oropharynx cancer is staged as two different diseases. HPV-positive (p16+) tumors do much better stage for stage, so AJCC 8 gave them their own, less severe system. Step one is always: what's the p16?

p16 positive
Its own system
  • T0 exists (p16+ node, no primary found)
  • Clinical N uses laterality and the 6 cm cutoff
  • Pathologic N uses node count
  • ENE is not used
  • Stages I-IV only
p16 negative
Same as oral cavity / larynx
  • T4 splits into T4a and T4b
  • N uses number, size, side, and ENE
  • Stages I-IVC
Same tumor, two stages

A 2.5 cm tonsil tumor with three ipsilateral nodes, the largest 3.5 cm, no ENE:

If p16+
T2 N1 → Stage I

Any number of ipsilateral nodes ≤6 cm is still cN1.

If p16-
T2 N2b → Stage IVA

Multiple ipsilateral nodes = N2b, and any N2 is at least IVA.

p16 only counts in the oropharynx (and unknown primaries with a neck node). A p16+ oral tongue cancer is still staged as oral cavity.

Nasopharynx: Where It Spread, Side, and Height

  • T-stage follows where the tumor has spread, not its size: soft tissue (parapharyngeal) = T2, bone (skull base) = T3, intracranial or cranial nerve = T4.
  • N-stage follows side and height: unilateral = N1, bilateral = N2, and >6 cm or below the cricoid = N3. Node count doesn't matter.

Larynx: Cord Mobility and Cartilage

  • Impaired cord mobility is T2; a fixed cord, paraglottic or pre-epiglottic space, or inner thyroid cartilage = T3.
  • Through the outer thyroid cartilage, cricoid, or outside the larynx = T4a.

Stage Is Not Treatment

Stage summarizes how far the disease has spread and the prognosis. Treatment is decided by the stage plus the primary site, resectability, expected function, pathology, the patient's health and wishes, and the treatment strategy being used.

This matters most in HPV-positive oropharynx cancer. The tonsil cancer above is stage I if p16-positive, but with three positive nodes it is still treated as locally advanced disease, often with chemoradiation. A lower stage number reflects a better prognosis; it does not by itself mean less treatment.

Self-check: two patients are both stage III. Why might one get surgery and the other chemoradiation?▾

Because stage is only one input. A stage III oral tongue cancer is resectable and usually goes to surgery first. A stage III larynx cancer with a working larynx is often treated with chemoradiation to preserve the larynx. Same stage, different site, function, and strategy.

Quick, straightforward TNM questions. Pick an answer, then read why. Use the tables below if you get stuck.

High-Yield Summary
  • The workup runs from exam and scope to biopsy with p16 when needed, imaging, pathology, a functional assessment with dental evaluation, staging, and a tumor board decision.
  • For non-HPV sites, N1 is a single ipsilateral node 3 cm or less, N2 is larger, multiple, or bilateral nodes, and N3 is a node over 6 cm or clinically obvious ENE.
  • In the oral cavity, depth of invasion drives T-stage, with cutoffs at 5 mm and 10 mm.
  • In the oropharynx, check p16 first, and in the nasopharynx, T-stage follows where the tumor spread and N-stage follows side and height.
  • Stage is not treatment: the plan depends on the stage plus the site, resectability, function, pathology, and the patient.

Treatment Paradigms.title: Treatment Paradigms Across Head & Neck Subsites
Treatment Paradigms.html:
This is where everything comes together: the subsite, the anatomy, the nodes, the imaging, and the stage. Don't memorize a separate algorithm for every site. Carry four questions into every new patient, then add the site's own twist.

1
Where is the primary?
→
2
Is it resectable?
→
3
Any adverse features?
→
4
What does RT need to treat?

The Four Questions

The highlighted phrases are what you look for in the chart, on imaging, and in the path report.

The H&N treatment framework

Go top to bottom. Question 3 only applies after surgery.

1
Where is the primary?
Oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx, hypopharynx, or nasopharynx
The subsite sets the biology, nodal drainage, surgical options, radiation field, and staging system.
Oral cavity leans toward surgery, oropharynx and larynx have real surgery-or-radiation choices, and the nasopharynx is treated with radiation.
2
Is it resectable, with acceptable function afterward?
Resectable, or not resectable / unfit
Resectable: surgery (en bloc resection with negative margins) ± neck dissection, and the pathology decides what comes next.
Not resectable or unfit: definitive radiation (about 70 Gy) ± concurrent systemic therapy, usually cisplatin.
"Resectable" also means the operation leaves the patient able to speak and swallow. When surgery would cost too much function, definitive chemoradiation is often preferred even if the tumor could technically be removed.
3
After surgery, what does the path report show?
pT3-T4, pN2-3, PNI, LVSI, or a close margin
Postoperative radiation (about 60 Gy).
These features predict local and regional recurrence if surgery alone is used. Observation is reasonable when none are present.
Positive margin or ENE
Postoperative chemoradiation: add concurrent cisplatin.
These are the two highest-risk features, and the only ones where adding chemo clearly helped in the landmark trials (RTOG 9501 / EORTC 22931, below).
4
What does the radiation actually need to treat?
Gross disease, high-risk regions, elective nodes
Define targets and organs at risk: the GTV, CTVs, and PTV, plus the normal structures to protect.
This is the step that turns a treatment decision into a radiation plan. See the next section.
Try it: pT2 N1 oral tongue cancer, negative margins, no ENE, but perineural invasion. What's next?▾

Postoperative radiation alone. PNI is an adverse feature, but there is no positive margin and no ENE, so no chemo.

Try it: same patient, but the path now shows ENE in one node. What changes?▾

Postoperative chemoradiation. ENE is one of the two highest-risk features, so concurrent cisplatin is added to postoperative radiation.

What a Head & Neck Radiation Plan Looks Like

You don't need to contour on a sub-I, but you should know what the team is drawing. Every plan has targets nested inside each other, and organs at risk wrapped tightly around them.

PTVThe CTVs plus a few millimeters for daily setup variation
CTV electiveNodal levels at risk for occult disease; lower dose
CTV high riskMargin around gross disease, or the surgical bed; highest risk of microscopic spread
GTVGross tumor and involved nodes you can see on exam or imaging; full dose
While protecting
  • Parotids
  • Submandibular glands
  • Oral cavity
  • Pharyngeal constrictors
  • Larynx
  • Mandible
  • Spinal cord
  • Brainstem
  • Cochlea
  • Optic structures (when nearby)
  • Brachial plexus (low neck)
Head and neck IMRT is a balancing act: cover several irregular targets with enough dose while keeping dose low in the structures responsible for swallowing, saliva, speech, hearing, and neurologic function.

Numbers You'll Hear on Rounds

SettingTypical regimen
Definitive70 Gy in 35 fractions to gross disease, with lower doses to the high-risk and elective volumes in the same plan
Postoperative60 Gy in 30 fractions; boost toward 66 Gy for a positive margin or ENE
Elective nodesA lower dose, commonly about 50 to 56 Gy
Concurrent chemoCisplatin, weekly or every 3 weeks. If cisplatin can't be given, the team picks an alternative (such as carboplatin-based chemo or cetuximab)

You don't need site-specific dose schedules (like the hypofractionated regimens for early glottic cancer). Know the big numbers and when chemo is added.

Oral Cavity

Resectable → surgery first, almost always. Radiation alone controls oral cavity cancer less well and puts the mandible at risk. The pathology then decides between observation, postoperative RT, and postoperative chemoradiation (Question 3).

  • The neck is dissected even when it looks clinically negative, because occult nodes are common once the tumor is more than a few millimeters deep.
  • Why the pathology matters so much here: the surgical specimen tells you the margins, DOI, PNI, LVSI, and ENE, which no scan can.
Tata Memorial (elective neck)

In early oral cancer with a clinically negative neck, elective neck dissection improved survival compared with watching the neck.

RTOG 9501 + EORTC 22931

Adding cisplatin to postoperative RT helped high-risk patients; a pooled analysis found a consistent benefit only for ENE and/or positive margins.

Oropharynx

The site with the most real choices, and the one you'll see most often in clinic.

Early disease (T1-T2, limited nodes)

Option 1
Transoral robotic surgery (TORS) + neck dissection

Removes the tumor through the mouth and gives full pathology. Some patients need no RT, or a lower adjuvant dose. The risk: unfavorable pathology can still require postoperative RT or chemoradiation.

Option 2
Definitive radiation

Treats the primary and the neck without an operation. Cure rates are similar. The tradeoff is radiation toxicity: dry mouth, taste change, and swallowing effects.

Avoid triple therapy. If the imaging already suggests the path will show ENE or a tight margin (for example, matted nodes or a deep tumor), TORS will likely be followed by both radiation and chemo. Definitive chemoradiation gets the same cure with one less treatment.

Locally advanced disease

Definitive chemoradiation (70 Gy with concurrent cisplatin) is the most common approach. Surgery followed by postoperative RT or chemoradiation is an option for selected patients, and induction chemo is used in some cases.

HPV-positive disease

Better prognosis and a different staging system, but do not equate a favorable prognosis with automatically reduced treatment. Off a clinical trial, HPV-positive patients get the same standard treatment, because the de-escalation strategies tested so far have not been safe enough to replace it.

RTOG 1016 + De-ESCALaTE

For HPV-positive oropharynx cancer, swapping cisplatin for cetuximab gave worse survival and more recurrences, without meaningfully less toxicity.

Larynx

The central question is not "can we avoid surgery?" It is "can we preserve a functional larynx?" A larynx that's kept but can't protect the airway or allow swallowing is not a success.

SituationUsual approach
Early glottic (T1-T2 N0)Definitive RT to the larynx alone (no elective neck) or transoral larynx-preserving surgery, chosen by tumor location, voice goals, and patient factors
Early supraglotticDefinitive RT including both sides of the neck, or partial laryngectomy with neck dissection
Locally advanced, larynx still worksConcurrent chemoradiation as an organ-preservation strategy, with total laryngectomy kept for salvage
Destroyed or nonfunctional larynx (cartilage destruction, T4a, poor airway or swallow)Total laryngectomy + neck dissection, then postoperative RT or chemoradiation
VA Larynx

Induction chemo followed by RT matched laryngectomy for survival, and about two-thirds of patients kept their larynx.

RTOG 91-11

Concurrent cisplatin-RT gave the best larynx preservation of the three arms. The main endpoint was keeping the larynx; overall survival was similar.

Nasopharynx

Why NPC is different
Radiation is the main treatment
  • The tumor is hard to resect well, tucked under the skull base
  • It spreads along the skull base and cranial nerves
  • It has extensive, bilateral nodal drainage (retropharyngeal, II, V)
  • It is radiosensitive and chemo-sensitive
  • EBV biology gives a blood marker (plasma EBV DNA)
How it's treated
By stage
  • Early (T1 N0): RT alone to the nasopharynx and the elective neck
  • Locally advanced: RT with concurrent cisplatin, often with induction chemo first
  • The neck, including level V and retropharyngeal nodes, is treated on both sides
  • Surgery: mainly for salvage of residual or recurrent disease

Hypopharynx

The worst prognosis of the major sites: it presents late, usually with nodes. It follows the same larynx-preservation logic as the larynx: chemoradiation or induction chemo for a functional larynx, and surgery (laryngopharyngectomy) for T4a disease.

Radiation Toxicity: Know What You're Trying to Prevent

Every organ at risk in the plan maps to a side effect you'll counsel patients about. Knowing that link is what makes the plan make sense.

Acute (during and just after RT)
  • Mucositis and painful swallowing
  • Dysphagia
  • Radiation dermatitis
  • Dry mouth and thick saliva
  • Taste change
  • Weight loss and dehydration
  • Risk of treatment breaks, which cost tumor control
Late (months to years)
  • Xerostomia
  • Dysphagia and aspiration
  • Neck fibrosis and lymphedema
  • Trismus
  • Dental caries
  • Osteoradionecrosis
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Hearing loss (site and cisplatin dependent)
  • Carotid stenosis in some patients
Dose to...Drives...
Parotids (and submandibular glands)Xerostomia, and the dental decay that follows
Oral cavityMucositis, taste loss, dental problems
Pharyngeal constrictorsDysphagia and aspiration
LarynxEdema, voice change, aspiration
MandibleOsteoradionecrosis
ThyroidHypothyroidism (check TSH in follow-up)
CochleaHearing loss, especially with cisplatin
Spinal cord, brainstem, optic structures, brachial plexusRare but serious nerve injury, so these have strict limits
PARSPORT

Parotid-sparing IMRT caused much less xerostomia than older conventional RT, without worse tumor control.

Prevention Starts Before Day One

  • Dental extractions before RT, then fluoride for life, to lower the risk of osteoradionecrosis.
  • Nutrition and swallowing support from the start; keep the patient swallowing during treatment.
  • No treatment breaks: tumor repopulation means delays cost cure.
  • Stop smoking: smoking during RT worsens both control and toxicity.

M1Platinum-based chemo (e.g., gemcitabine/cisplatin) ± immunotherapy; consider RT to the primary and neck if there's a good response.

Surgery is used only for salvage (e.g., residual neck disease or a local recurrence).

High-Yield Summary
  • Ask four questions for every patient: where is the primary, is it resectable, what are the adverse features after surgery, and what does the radiation need to treat.
  • After surgery, adverse features such as pT3 to T4, multiple nodes, PNI, LVSI, or a close margin call for radiation to about 60 Gy, and a positive margin or ENE adds concurrent cisplatin.
  • Definitive treatment is about 70 Gy in 35 fractions to gross disease, with lower doses to high-risk and elective volumes, while sparing the parotids, constrictors, mandible, cord, and brainstem.
  • Early oropharynx cancer can be treated with TORS or radiation, and the team should avoid triple therapy; HPV-positive disease is not de-escalated off trial.
  • The larynx question is whether a functional larynx can be preserved, and the nasopharynx is treated with radiation and chemo because surgery has a limited role.
